definition: A military artificial intelligence arms race is a technological, economic, and military competition between two or more states to develop and deploy advanced AI technologies and lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS).
details: The goal is to gain a strategic or tactical advantage over rivals, similar to previous arms races involving nuclear or conventional military technologies. Since the mid-2010s, many analysts have noted the emergence of such an arms race between superpowers for better AI technology and military AI, driven by increasing geopolitical and military tensions. An AI arms race is sometimes placed in the context of an AI Cold War between the United States and China. Several influential figures and publications have emphasized that whoever develops artificial general intelligence (AGI) first could dominate global affairs in the 21st century. Russian President Vladimir Putin stated that the leader in AI will "rule the world." Researchers and experts, such as Leopold Aschenbrenner and Adrian Pecotic respectively, warn that the AGI race between major powers like the U.S. and China could reshape geopolitical power. This includes AI for surveillance, autonomous weapons, decision-making systems, cyber operations, and more.

explainer.lead: An AI arms race is a competition between states to build and deploy more capable military AI before their rivals do. It matters because the contest could affect military power and global politics, from surveillance and cyber operations to autonomous weapons.

tiers.eli5: Imagine two countries each building a faster, cleverer robot helper for their armies because they worry the other will get ahead. Each new advance pushes the other to respond, much like earlier competitions over weapons. The goal is an advantage, but the contest can also increase tension between rivals.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers may encounter this competition in military and national-security work on surveillance, autonomous weapons, decision-making systems, and cyber operations. The central pitfall is treating technical leadership as a simple finish line: the concept covers development and deployment across many systems, with AGI as one possible focus rather than a requirement.
tiers.paperLevel: For states S = {S1, ..., Sn}, a military AI arms race is technological, economic, and military competition to develop and deploy advanced AI and lethal autonomous weapons systems in pursuit of strategic or tactical advantage. Since the mid-2010s, analysts have increasingly described such competition among superpowers, often in the context of US–China rivalry. The term does not imply that AGI is necessary or that advantage can be reduced to one technical capability.

explainer.example: Suppose one state introduces more capable AI-assisted military surveillance. A rival, fearing a loss of situational awareness, expands its own surveillance AI and autonomous-weapons programmes; the first state then responds in turn, creating a competitive cycle.

explainer.intuition: Rivals invest in military AI because each fears falling behind, and one state's advances can encourage others to accelerate their own efforts. The underlying aim is strategic or tactical advantage, much as in earlier nuclear and conventional arms races.
howItWorks: Two or more states seek an advantage through advanced AI technology.
They compete technologically, economically, and militarily to develop and deploy relevant systems.
Applications can include surveillance, autonomous weapons, decision support, and cyber operations.
Rival progress and geopolitical tension encourage further investment and deployment.
Some participants also treat leadership in AGI as a possible route to wider global influence.
explainer.whyItMatters: The competition could reshape military capabilities and geopolitical power, particularly between major rivals such as the United States and China. It also connects technical progress with broader questions about autonomous weapons and international security.
misconceptions: It is not only a race to build AGI; existing military AI and autonomous weapons are also central.
It is not limited to building better models, because economic and military development and deployment are part of the competition.
The AI Cold War framing is one interpretation, not a separate technical definition of the arms race.
